vignette:
Arjun's Case

Arjun was thirty years old when he came to the clinic, though the exhaustion in his face made him look older. He had owned the corner grocery store on Elmhurst for six years—a modest, steady business that his family had helped him establish—and it was there, in the fluorescent-lit aisles among the familiar inventory, that his life had begun to fracture two years ago. His then-partner, Marcus, had been controlling and volatile. What started as jealousy about Arjun's attention to customers had escalated over months into accusations and isolation. One evening in the stockroom, after Arjun had mentioned wanting to spend a weekend with his brother, Marcus had shoved him hard against the metal shelving. When Arjun tried to push back, Marcus had beaten him methodically—fists to his ribs, his shoulders, his face—while hissing that Arjun was ungrateful, that no one else would want him. Arjun had frozen partway through, his body seeming to betray him, and that paralysis haunted him as much as the violence itself. He had stayed for another six months before finally leaving.

Since then, Arjun's world had contracted in ways he could not entirely explain to himself. The stockroom where it happened was now a space he could barely enter; he hired a part-time assistant to handle most of the restocking, which cut into his margins. But the problem was far larger than the physical location. His body had become a stranger to him, a thing that betrayed him without warning. When a male customer approached the counter—particularly if the man was tall, broad-shouldered, wore cologne that mingled with natural sweat—Arjun's chest would tighten and his hands would shake slightly as he rang up their items. The smell of sweat was the worst trigger. It would catapult him backward into the stockroom, the memory arriving with such force and vividness that he could feel Marcus's hands on him again, could taste the metallic blood in his mouth. Once, a regular customer had come in after the gym, and the moment Arjun caught that acrid, human scent, the full memory of the assault crashed through him without warning—the weight of the fists, the helplessness, the rage at himself for freezing. Each time the smell returned—sweat, cologne, the particular musk of an unfamiliar man—Arjun found himself thinking with a logic that felt inescapable: This is what my body does now. It betrays me. I cannot trust it. The sensory trigger had become inseparable from his conviction that he was fundamentally broken. He had excused himself to the bathroom and sat on the floor for twenty minutes, trembling. After the memory had surfaced with such force, even the smallest sensory details began to feel laden with threat: the particular fluorescent hum of the stockroom lights, the metallic clink of a shelf being adjusted, the way certain customers moved through the aisles with an ease he no longer possessed. His mind had learned to scan for these echoes, to treat them as warnings.

Over the following months, Arjun had come to believe that his body could not be trusted. It kept reacting as though danger was imminent even when he was standing safely behind his register, even when the customer was harmless. Once he had settled into this conviction—that his body was fundamentally unreliable, that he would freeze again if truly threatened—almost any male presence in the store began to feel like a potential test of that fragility. The belief that he could not protect himself meant that ordinary customer interactions, things that had once been routine, now snagged his attention and held it: the tall man in the blue jacket, the deep voice asking for directions, even the innocent brush of a shoulder as someone passed by the counter. His vigilance at night had intensified; he could fall asleep around eight or nine, but would jolt awake at two or three in the morning, convinced someone was outside his apartment door. He had installed a second lock, then a third. He had come to feel certain that he could not rely on himself—that his body's paralysis during the assault proved something fundamentally broken in him, something that meant he would fail again if threatened. This conviction fed back into his perception of danger; when a stranger walked in, his mind immediately cycled through scenarios: What if he becomes aggressive? What if I freeze again? What if I can't protect myself? The belief that he was damaged, that his body could not be trusted, meant that ordinary moments began to feel loaded with threat—the tall man in the blue jacket, the deep voice asking for directions, even the innocent brush of a shoulder as someone passed by the counter now snagged his attention as potential confirmations of danger. The threat felt enormous, omnipresent, even though rationally he knew most people were not violent. His certainty that he was damaged, that his body would betray him, transformed how he read the world; it meant that ambiguity—a customer's neutral expression, a raised voice over a pricing question, even the ordinary jostle of the lunch-hour rush—became something he could not afford to dismiss, each moment a potential confirmation of the danger he was convinced lurked beneath the surface.

Certain conversation topics—when customers or his few remaining friends mentioned relationships, trust, or strength—would trigger a cascade of shame and rage. The rage was the most confusing part. When the memory surfaced, usually unbidden and complete, Arjun felt not fear but a burning fury directed entirely at himself. He would clench his fists and think, I should have fought harder. I should have done more. I will never forgive myself for just lying there. This rage would then amplify his sense of threat; he would become irritable, short with customers, convinced that people could see his weakness and would exploit it. His current partner, Deepak, had noticed the withdrawal, the way Arjun flinched at unexpected touch, the nights he lay awake beside him. Deepak had tried to help, but Arjun's conviction that he could not be relied upon extended to relationships—he was certain he would eventually fail Deepak too, that his damaged body and fractured mind made him a liability. When Deepak suggested they go out to a restaurant or a bar, Arjun would decline. The thought of being in a crowded space, surrounded by strangers whose intentions he could not predict, where his body might betray him again, felt impossible.

What had finally pushed Arjun to seek help was not a single crisis but an accumulation: the business suffering because he could not function in his own space, his relationship straining under the weight of his avoidance and self-recrimination, and the exhaustion of living in a state of constant vigilance. He sat in the intake session with his hands folded tightly in his lap, and when asked what he most feared, he said quietly: "That I'll always be like this. That I'll hurt the people I love by being too broken to be there for them." What he hoped for, though he said it almost as an afterthought, was simply to walk into his stockroom without his heart racing, and to believe that his body might someday feel like his own again.
